articles.title: Domain Name Broker: Do You Need One to Sell a Domain?
articles.description: Should you hire a domain name broker to sell your domain? Learn what domain brokers do, how much they charge, and when it makes financial sense to use one.

sections.heading: Overview
body: A domain name broker is a specialist who manages the valuation, buyer outreach, negotiation, and transfer of premium domain sales on your behalf. Brokers charge 10–20% commission and are most valuable for domains worth $5,000 or more where active outreach to qualified buyers can dramatically increase sale price. For domains under $5,000, self-service marketplace listing on Sedo or Afternic is typically more cost-efficient.

sections.heading: What Does a Domain Name Broker Do?
body: A domain name broker is a specialized professional who facilitates the sale (or purchase) of domain names on behalf of clients. They serve as an intermediary between buyers and sellers, handling everything from initial outreach to final transfer.
Core Services a Domain Broker Provides

Valuation and pricing strategy: An experienced broker has seen hundreds or thousands of domain sales. They can tell you where your domain sits in the market and help you set a price that's ambitious but realistic — a balance that's harder to strike than it sounds.

Buyer outreach: Instead of listing your domain and waiting for an inbound inquiry, brokers actively reach out to potential buyers. They identify companies in relevant industries, individuals who might covet the name, and existing investors who've expressed interest in similar domains. This outbound approach can dramatically accelerate a sale.

Negotiation: This is where brokers earn their commission. Professional domain brokers are skilled negotiators who understand market dynamics, buyer psychology, and deal structure. They know when to hold firm and when to be flexible, and they negotiate without the emotional attachment that individual sellers often bring to the table.

Confidential representation: Many sellers prefer to keep their identity private during negotiations. A broker can approach buyers on your behalf without revealing who owns the domain — preventing the buyer from using that information to gain a negotiating advantage.

Legal and administrative handling: Brokers typically manage the escrow process, transfer documentation, and post-sale administration. This protects both parties and reduces the risk of errors that could complicate a transaction.

sections.heading: How Domain Broker Fees Work
body: Understanding domain broker fee structures upfront is essential to evaluating whether hiring one makes financial sense for your situation.
Commission-Based Structure
Most domain brokers work on a commission basis — they take a percentage of the final sale price, collected only when the deal closes. Typical commission rates:
10–15% for mid-range domains ($5,000–$50,000)
10–20% for premium domains (above $50,000)
15–25% for entry-level broker services or smaller deals
Some brokers charge a lower commission rate but add a flat fee for services like outreach campaigns, professional photography of certificates, or appraisal documents.
Retainer Fees

Some brokers — especially those handling very high-value domains — charge an upfront retainer fee in addition to or instead of a commission. This retainer covers the time and resources they invest in outreach and negotiation before any sale is guaranteed.
Retainers are more common when:
The broker is expected to run an active outreach campaign
The domain requires significant research to identify the right buyers
The expected transaction size is large enough to justify the investment
Flat-Fee Models

A few emerging broker services operate on a flat-fee or subscription model rather than commission. These can be cost-effective for sellers with multiple domains or those who want predictable costs. The downside is that flat-fee brokers may have less incentive to maximize your sale price.

sections.heading: When Does It Make Sense to Hire a Domain Broker?
body: Your Domain Is Worth $5,000 or More

For domains valued under $5,000, broker commissions can consume a significant portion of your proceeds. A 15% commission on a $2,000 sale is $300 — meaningful, but manageable if the broker saves you time and achieves a higher price. Below $1,000, self-selling through marketplaces like Sedo or Afternic is almost always more economical.

For domains worth $5,000, $10,000, $50,000, or more, a broker's expertise can add value that far exceeds their commission. A skilled broker who negotiates your $20,000 asking price up to $35,000 while charging 15% ($5,250) has net-added $9,750 to your proceeds compared to a self-managed sale.
You Don't Know How to Find Buyers

Listing a domain on a marketplace and waiting is a passive strategy. It works for many domains — but for premium names, the most qualified buyers (large companies, well-funded startups, strategic acquirers) rarely browse Afternic. Brokers with industry relationships can get your domain in front of decision-makers who have both the budget and the need.
Negotiations Make You Uncomfortable

Domain negotiation can get complicated and emotionally charged, especially if a buyer is aggressive or the offer comes with unusual terms. If negotiation isn't your strength, a broker insulates you from the dynamics that can cause sellers to either fold too quickly or hold out unreasonably.
You Want to Maintain Confidentiality

If your name is attached to the domain (through WHOIS or public records) and you'd prefer buyers not know who's selling, a broker provides a confidential buffer. This is particularly valuable for corporate sellers who don't want competitors or the press to know they're divesting a domain.
You're Managing a Portfolio, Not a Single Domain

If you have multiple premium domains to sell, a broker relationship can be highly efficient. Many brokers offer portfolio representation, actively marketing your entire collection to relevant buyers rather than waiting for individual inquiries.
Key Facts for 2026:

Domains sold through professional brokers achieve sale prices that are, on average, 40–60% higher than comparable domains sold through self-service marketplaces, according to transaction data from major brokerages — with the difference most pronounced for domains above $20,000.

The top five domain brokerages collectively handled over $500 million in domain transactions in 2025, reflecting the continued concentration of premium domain sales through professional intermediaries.

Broker commission rates have compressed slightly over the past decade: rates that were 20–25% in 2015 are now typically 10–15% for mid-market domains, driven by marketplace competition and more transparent market pricing data.

Approximately 30% of all domain sales above $50,000 are completed through a broker rather than a marketplace, reflecting the complexity and buyer-identification challenges unique to ultra-premium transactions.

sections.heading: When You Don't Need a Domain Broker
body: The Domain Is Listed on an Active Marketplace

Sedo, Afternic, and Dan.com have built infrastructure specifically designed to connect buyers and sellers without needing a broker. If your domain is priced in the $500–$5,000 range and is well-suited to these platforms, self-listing is a perfectly viable strategy.
You Already Know the Buyer

If a specific company has already approached you about buying your domain, or if you have a clear sense of who the ideal buyer is and how to reach them, you may be able to negotiate directly without a broker's help.
You're Not in a Rush
Brokers accelerate sales through active outreach. If you're happy to list and wait — checking in periodically and being patient — you can achieve good results without commission costs.

sections.heading: How to Find a Reputable Domain Name Broker
body: Major Domain Brokerages
Sedo Brokerage Service — Sedo is not just a marketplace; it operates a professional brokerage team that handles acquisition and sale campaigns for premium domains. Their network is genuinely global.

GoDaddy Premium Domain Broker — GoDaddy offers a concierge domain acquisition service for buyers wanting to pursue taken domains, and a brokerage service for sellers of premium names. The platform's size gives brokers broad market access.
MediaOptions — one of the most respected independent domain brokerages, specializing in premium generic .com domains. Known for discretion and strong negotiating outcomes.
Grit Brokerage — a newer player with strong reputation in the startup and tech domain space, particularly for .io and .ai domains.
DomainAgents — connects buyers and sellers for targeted domain acquisitions, operating on a fee-per-inquiry model.
What to Look for in a Domain Broker
Verifiable track record: Ask for examples of comparable sales they've closed
Transparent fee structure: No hidden fees or vague commission language
Clear communication: They should be easy to reach and responsive
Market specialization: Some brokers specialize in tech, others in generic .com — match their expertise to your domain type
References: Established brokers should have satisfied clients willing to speak on their behalf

sections.heading: A Hybrid Approach: List Yourself + Broker for Serious Offers
body: One underused strategy: list your domain on self-serve marketplaces at a "buy now" price, but engage a broker for any offer above a certain threshold. This way, you capture motivated impulse buyers yourself (without commission) while having professional support for the high-value negotiations that benefit most from expertise.

sections.heading: The Bottom Line
body: For everyday domains in the sub-$5,000 range, self-service platforms are usually sufficient. For premium domains worth five figures or more — especially those requiring active outreach, confidential representation, or sophisticated negotiation — a domain name broker more than earns their commission.

The right broker brings market intelligence, buyer relationships, and negotiation skills to your sale that are genuinely difficult to replicate as an individual. Just make sure you vet them carefully, understand the fee structure upfront, and choose someone whose track record aligns with your domain type.
Research domain values, explore the market, and find available names at every price point. Use DomainsDiscovery.com to check domain availability and compare prices across registrars instantly.

sections.heading: Expert Verdict
body: The decision to use a domain broker is fundamentally a financial optimization problem. At its core, it requires estimating the incremental sale price a broker's expertise and buyer network will generate, and comparing that against their commission. For domains below $5,000, the math rarely works in favor of a broker. For domains above $20,000, the math almost always does — because the percentage uplift a skilled broker achieves on a $50,000 domain (often 40–60% above what a passive marketplace listing yields) is worth multiples of the 10–15% commission.

The less obvious value of a domain broker is in buyer discovery. This is where professional brokers create the most asymmetric value relative to their fee. Domain marketplaces are passive infrastructure — they expose your domain to buyers who are already searching for domains. But the most qualified buyers for a premium domain — the VP of Marketing at a Fortune 500 company, the recently funded founder who needs to upgrade their brand, the PE-backed company executing a rebrand — are not browsing Afternic. They are reachable only through direct outreach by someone with the right industry relationships and the professionalism to engage corporate decision-makers. This is precisely what top brokers provide.

The diligence framework for choosing a broker is straightforward: ask for three to five comparable completed sales with verifiable transaction details, request references from sellers of domains similar in type and price range to yours, and insist on a written engagement agreement with clear commission terms, duration, and exit clauses. A broker confident in their capabilities will readily provide all of this. One who deflects or hedges on any of these points is a broker to avoid.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
body:
Q: What does a domain name broker charge?
A: Domain broker commissions typically range from 10–15% for mid-range domains ($5,000–$50,000) and 10–20% for premium domains above $50,000. Entry-level broker services and smaller transactions may carry 15–25% commissions. Some brokers also charge upfront retainer fees for active outreach campaigns. Always request a complete fee breakdown in writing before signing an engagement agreement.

Q: Is it worth hiring a domain broker for a $10,000 domain?
A: Yes, in most cases. A broker charging 15% commission on a $10,000 domain costs $1,500. If their active outreach and negotiation skills achieve a final sale price of $14,000 instead of $10,000, you net $1,400 more than a self-managed sale — and save significant time. The break-even calculation depends on whether the broker can reliably achieve a higher sale price, which is why verifying comparable completed sales before hiring is essential.

Q: How do I know if a domain broker is legitimate?
A: Legitimate brokers can provide: verifiable examples of comparable completed sales (with domain names and approximate prices), client references you can contact directly, a transparent written fee agreement, and membership or affiliation with recognized domain industry organizations. Avoid brokers who cannot provide completed sale examples, demand large upfront fees before any outreach begins, or make specific price guarantees they cannot support with data.

Q: Can a domain broker help me buy a domain I want?
A: Yes. Acquisition brokerage is a major part of many brokers' businesses. They research domain ownership, make discreet initial contact on your behalf, negotiate the purchase price without revealing your budget or identity, and handle escrow and transfer. GoDaddy's concierge acquisition service, Sedo's brokerage team, and DomainAgents all offer buyer-side representation. Acquisition broker fees are typically structured as commission on the final purchase price or a flat fee per successful acquisition.

Q: What is the difference between a domain marketplace and a domain broker?
A: A marketplace (Sedo, Afternic, Dan.com) is passive infrastructure — you list your domain, set a price, and wait for inbound buyers to find it. A broker actively identifies and approaches potential buyers on your behalf. Marketplaces charge 9–20% commission for transactions facilitated through their platform. Brokers charge similar percentages but add the value of outbound buyer discovery, which is particularly important for premium domains that qualified buyers wouldn't encounter through passive marketplace browsing.

Q: How long does it take a broker to sell a domain?
A: Most reputable brokers set expectations of 3–12 months for a premium domain sale. Active outreach begins within the first month; initial responses from potential buyers typically arrive within 30–60 days; negotiations, escrow, and transfer can add another 30–60 days after an offer is accepted. Brokers with strong existing buyer networks in your domain's category tend to transact faster than generalist brokers without pre-established relationships.

Q: What should I ask a domain broker before signing an agreement?
A: Ask: (1) What comparable domains have you sold in the last 12 months and at what price? (2) Who are your current buyers and investors in this category? (3) What is your outreach strategy for finding qualified buyers for my domain? (4) What are the exact commission and fee terms, and are there cancellation provisions? (5) What is your typical time-to-sale for domains in this price range? A broker who cannot answer all five questions thoroughly is not yet ready for your listing. --- ``json { "@context": "https://schema.org", "@type": "FAQPage", "mainEntity": [ { "@type": "Question", "name": "What does a domain name broker charge?", "acceptedAnswer": { "@type": "Answer", "text": "Domain broker commissions typically range from 10–15% for mid-range domains ($5,000–$50,000) and 10–20% for premium domains above $50,000. articles.title: Afternic vs Sedo: Which Domain Marketplace Gets You More?
articles.description: Afternic vs Sedo: comparing the two biggest domain marketplaces on fees, reach, and seller tools to help you decide the best place to sell your domain.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Afternic charges 20% commission but offers unmatched distribution through 100+ partner registrars including GoDaddy. Sedo charges only 15% commission and adds domain parking revenue plus strong international reach. For most sellers, listing on both platforms simultaneously delivers the best Afternic vs Sedo results.

sections.heading: What Is Afternic?
body: Afternic is a domain marketplace owned by GoDaddy, the world's largest domain registrar. It was founded in 1999 and has since built one of the most extensive distribution networks in the industry. When you list a domain on Afternic, it can appear across more than 100 partner registrars, including GoDaddy itself, Namecheap, and Network Solutions.
Key Features of Afternic
Distribution network: Your domain listing appears on partner registrar searches automatically
Fast Transfer domains: Domains registered at GoDaddy or transferred to Afternic can be sold and transferred in minutes
Premium listings: Afternic promotes high-value domains in front of buyers actively searching
Integrated pricing tools: Sellers get suggested pricing based on comparable sales data
Brokerage service: For high-value domains, Afternic offers negotiation support

Afternic's biggest strength is its GoDaddy integration. Because GoDaddy powers a massive share of global domain searches, your listing gets visibility at the exact moment buyers are looking for names.

sections.heading: What Is Sedo?
body: Sedo (Search Engine for Domain Offers) is a German-founded marketplace launched in 2001. It operates independently and has built its own international buyer network across more than 200 countries. Sedo handles over 18 million domains in its database and has facilitated some of the largest domain sales in history.
Key Features of Sedo
International reach: Particularly strong in European markets
Sedo Brokerage: Active broker team that negotiates on your behalf
Domain parking: Earn revenue from parked domains while they're listed for sale
Auction system: Run time-limited auctions to create urgency among buyers
SEO-friendly listings: Sedo's marketplace pages are indexed by search engines, driving organic buyer traffic

Sedo's parking program is a standout feature. While your domain sits for sale, Sedo displays relevant ads on it and shares the revenue with you. For high-traffic domains, this can generate meaningful income while you wait for the right buyer.

sections.heading: Afternic vs Sedo: Fee Comparison
body: Fees are often the deciding factor in a domain marketplace comparison. Here's how both platforms stack up.
Afternic Commission Rates
Standard listing: 20% commission on sale price
Premium listing: 20% commission (same rate, higher visibility)
GoDaddy-registered domains: Commission may vary depending on listing tier
Afternic's 20% commission applies regardless of whether the sale happens through their website or a partner registrar network. There's no listing fee to publish your domain.
Sedo Commission Rates
Standard sales: 15% commission (minimum $60)
Brokered sales: 15% commission
Domain parking: Revenue share varies by traffic
Sedo's 15% commission is lower than Afternic's 20%, which makes a meaningful difference on high-value sales. On a $10,000 domain, that's $500 extra in your pocket with Sedo.

sections.heading: Buyer Reach: Who Finds Your Domain?
body: Both platforms offer impressive reach, but through different channels.
Afternic's Distribution Network

Afternic wins on sheer distribution volume. When a buyer searches for a domain at GoDaddy and the name is taken, GoDaddy suggests Afternic listings as alternatives. This passive, high-intent traffic is extremely valuable. Buyers don't need to visit Afternic.com — they find your listing inside the registrar's own interface.
Sedo's Organic and Direct Traffic

Sedo attracts buyers who are specifically hunting for premium domains. Many experienced domain investors and businesses search Sedo directly. Its international reach also gives you access to European and Asian buyers who may not use GoDaddy as their primary registrar.

Verdict: For U.S.-focused domains and names tied to popular English keywords, Afternic's GoDaddy network gives you a major edge. For international domains or names with multilingual appeal, Sedo's global buyer pool is more valuable.

sections.heading: Listing and Management Tools
body: Afternic's Seller Dashboard

Afternic's interface is functional but straightforward. You can set your price, choose between Buy Now or Make Offer options, and view inquiry activity. The Fast Transfer badge (exclusive to GoDaddy-registered domains) significantly speeds up the closing process.
Sedo's Seller Dashboard

Sedo offers more detailed analytics on listing performance, including views and click data. You can also configure parking pages, run auctions, and access Sedo's brokerage team directly from the dashboard. The platform feels more seller-focused overall.

sections.heading: Which Platform Is Better for Different Sellers?
body: Best for Beginners: Afternic

If you're new to domain selling and your domains are registered at GoDaddy, Afternic is the simpler and more integrated choice. Setup takes minutes, and the passive distribution network does the marketing for you.
Best for Portfolio Sellers: Sedo
If you have a large portfolio and want to maximize revenue per sale, Sedo's lower commission rate and parking revenue make it the stronger financial play.
Best for Premium Domains: Both
For domains valued above $10,000, it's worth listing on both platforms simultaneously. Most sellers do exactly this — cross-listing increases exposure without much additional effort.

sections.heading: Practical Tips for Selling on Either Platform
body: 1. Set a realistic Buy Now price: Research comparable sales using NameBio before you set your ask
2. Enable Make Offer: This filters out low-ball buyers while keeping serious ones engaged
3. Use both platforms: Cross-listing is allowed and doubles your exposure
4. Write a strong listing description: Sedo lets you add context about the domain's use case — use it
5. Price in round numbers: Buyers respond better to $4,500 than $4,499 in the premium domain market

sections.heading: Real-World Examples
body: A .com domain related to financial planning sold on Afternic for $8,500 through GoDaddy's network — the buyer found it while searching for the exact name
A two-word .com with European traffic history sold on Sedo for €12,000 after Sedo's brokerage team reached out to a shortlist of qualified buyers
A portfolio seller running 200 domains reported that 60% of his sales came through Afternic's distribution network, while 30% came through Sedo

sections.heading: The Verdict: Afternic vs Sedo
body: There's no universal winner in the Afternic vs Sedo comparison — the best platform depends on your specific situation.
Commission — Afternic: 20% · Sedo: 15%
Distribution — Afternic: 100+ partners · Sedo: Global direct
Parking Revenue — Afternic: No · Sedo: Yes
International Reach — Afternic: Moderate · Sedo: Strong
Ease of Setup — Afternic: Easy · Sedo: Moderate
If maximizing passive distribution is your goal, go with Afternic. If you want lower fees and international reach with parking income on the side, Sedo gives you more tools.
For most serious domain sellers, the smartest move is listing on both.

sections.heading: Expert Verdict
body: Afternic and Sedo represent two fundamentally different philosophies for domain sales. Afternic is a distribution-first platform — its GoDaddy integration ensures your domain surfaces at the exact moment high-intent buyers are searching at the world's most popular registrar. This passive reach is difficult to replicate and explains why Afternic consistently drives high sales volume for .com domains with popular English keywords. The 20% commission is the price of that distribution engine.

Sedo, by contrast, is a marketplace-first platform that rewards sellers who want more control, lower commissions, and income from parked assets. For large portfolio holders managing dozens or hundreds of domains, Sedo's 5% commission advantage compounds meaningfully. A seller moving $200,000 in domain inventory annually saves $10,000 in commission by using Sedo instead of Afternic — a figure that far exceeds any productivity or convenience benefit.

The authoritative recommendation for serious domain sellers in 2026 is unambiguous: list on both. The platforms are free to list on, cross-listing is explicitly permitted, and the incremental effort is minimal compared to the exposure gains. Prioritize GoDaddy-registered domains on Afternic for Fast Transfer advantages, and use Sedo's brokerage team for your premium and internationally-appealing names.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
body:
Q: Is Afternic or Sedo better for selling a .com domain?
A: Afternic has the edge for .com domains, particularly those with popular English keywords. Its distribution through GoDaddy's network means your listing appears to millions of buyers searching for domain names at the point of purchase. However, for premium .coms above $10,000, both platforms should be used simultaneously.

Q: Can I list my domain on both Afternic and Sedo at the same time?
A: Yes. Cross-listing on multiple domain marketplaces is permitted and common practice. Listing on both Afternic and Sedo simultaneously increases your domain's exposure without additional cost, since both platforms are free to list on. Just ensure your pricing is consistent across both to avoid confusion.

Q: What is Sedo's minimum commission fee?
A: Sedo charges a minimum commission of $60 per transaction, even if 15% of the sale price would be less than that amount. This makes Sedo's economics less favorable for very low-priced domain sales (under $400), where the minimum fee effectively represents a higher percentage.

Q: Does Afternic charge listing fees?
A: No. Afternic charges no upfront listing fee. The 20% commission is deducted only when a domain sells. This means listing large portfolios on Afternic costs nothing until a sale occurs, making it a risk-free option for sellers building their first domain portfolio.

Q: How long does it take to sell a domain on these platforms?
A: Timelines vary widely. Hand-registered domains may sell in weeks or take years depending on demand. Industry data suggests the average domain sits listed for 6–18 months before selling. Premium domains with strong keywords tend to sell faster. Afternic's passive distribution can accelerate sales by reaching buyers who weren't actively looking at a marketplace.

Q: Does Sedo's domain parking actually generate revenue?
A: Sedo's parking program generates meaningful revenue only for domains with existing organic traffic. A domain receiving hundreds of monthly visitors can earn $20–$200+ per month through parking. For newly registered domains with no traffic, parking income is negligible. The program is most valuable for aged domains with established backlinks or direct type-in traffic.

Q: What is the best domain marketplace for international buyers?
A: Sedo is definitively stronger for international sales. Its 200-country buyer network and particularly deep penetration in European markets make it the preferred marketplace for sellers with domains that have multilingual appeal or country-code TLDs. Afternic's strength is concentrated primarily in English-language and U.S.-focused domains. ---

body: Before you list your domain for sale, you need to understand its market value — and that starts with knowing what similar domains are selling for and what's available right now.

Use DomainsDiscovery.com to check domain availability and compare prices across registrars instantly. Whether you're buying your first domain or building a portfolio to sell, DomainsDiscovery.com gives you the data you need to make smarter decisions from the start.

articles.title: How to Price Your Domain for Sale (Without Leaving Money Behind)
topics: how to price a domain for sale
articles.description: Learn how to price a domain for sale the right way. Avoid underpricing and overpricing with proven domain pricing strategies and real market data tips.

sections.heading: Overview
body: To price a domain for sale, research 5–10 comparable sales on NameBio, run an automated appraisal for a sanity check, estimate the end-user value to a real business, adjust for TLD (with .com commanding a premium), then set your asking price 10–30% above your target to leave room for negotiation.

sections.heading: Why Domain Pricing Is More Art Than Science
body: Unlike houses or cars, domains don't have a standardized appraisal system. Two domains that look similar on the surface — say, "BlueSkyMedia.com" and "ClearSkyMarketing.com" — can differ wildly in value based on factors that aren't immediately obvious. Length, keyword strength, search volume, industry demand, and even the current news cycle all play a role.
That said, pricing is absolutely something you can learn. The key is combining data with pattern recognition, and we'll show you both.

sections.heading: Step 1: Use NameBio to Research Comparable Sales
body: The most important tool for how to price a domain for sale is NameBio.com, a database of over 2 million domain sales. Before you list anything, search for domains that are similar to yours.
How to Search NameBio Effectively
Search by keyword: Enter a word that's in your domain and filter by TLD (.com, .net, etc.)
Sort by date: Focus on sales from the last 12–24 months — older data may not reflect current demand
Filter by price range: This helps you see where the market actually sits, not where sellers wish it was
Look at length: A 5-letter .com sells for very different amounts than a 12-character domain
What to Look for in Comparables
When you find comparable sales, ask yourself:
Is my domain shorter or longer than the comparable?
Does my domain have stronger or weaker keyword relevance?
Is the comparable a dictionary word, or a made-up term?
Was the sale recent or years ago?
Adjust your price up or down based on these factors. This is the foundation of any solid domain pricing strategy.

sections.heading: Step 2: Run Your Domain Through Automated Valuation Tools
body: Automated appraisal tools are imperfect — but they're a useful sanity check. They'll catch obvious overpricing before you embarrass yourself on a marketplace.
Best Domain Valuation Tools
GoDaddy Appraisal (EstiBot): Free, widely used, gives a ballpark estimate
Estibot.com: More detailed breakdown, good for understanding what factors drive the value
Sedo's Domain Appraisal: Useful if you plan to list on Sedo
DomainIndex: Aggregates multiple data points including search volume and backlinks
Important caveat: Never rely solely on automated appraisals. These tools regularly undervalue strong brandable domains and overvalue keyword-stuffed garbage. Use them as one data point among several.

sections.heading: Step 3: Consider the End-User Value
body: The most important question in domain pricing is: who would buy this, and what would it be worth to them?

End users — real businesses, not domain investors — pay dramatically more than investors do. An investor buying to resell will offer you 10–20% of their estimated resale value. An end user who actually needs the domain to launch their business may pay full market value or more.
Example: Calculating End-User Value
Suppose you own "SolarRoofQuotes.com." Think about who would buy it:
A solar installation company trying to rank for "solar roof quotes" searches
A lead generation business in the solar space
A startup building a comparison platform for solar panels

Any of these buyers could see this domain as a traffic and branding asset worth thousands. If the domain could generate $500/month in leads, a business might value it at $10,000–$30,000 based on standard multiples.
This kind of thinking should anchor your domain listing price when you have a keyword-rich, industry-specific name.

sections.heading: Step 4: Factor in TLD and Domain Extension
body: Not all TLDs are created equal, and this has a massive impact on domain pricing strategy.
TLD Value Hierarchy (Approximate)
1. .com: Premium tier — always commands the highest prices
2. .net and .org: Strong, but typically 20–40% lower than .com equivalents
3. .io: Strong in tech/startup space, valued highly in that niche
4. .co: Decent, particularly for international or startup brands
5. Country codes (.uk, .de, .au): Valuable locally, limited global appeal
6. New TLDs (.app, .ai, .shop): Market is maturing but still secondary to .com
If you own "Finance.net," don't price it like "Finance.com." The .com extension carries a premium that can be 5x or more in the right market.

sections.heading: Step 5: Set Your Asking Price with Strategy
body: Now that you have your data, how do you actually set the number?
The Three-Price Framework
Before listing, define three numbers:
Your minimum: The absolute lowest you'd accept and walk away satisfied
Your target: The realistic price you expect based on market data
Your ask: What you list the domain for publicly (10–30% above target)
This gives you room to negotiate without regret. Most serious domain buyers will counter-offer, so pricing at your target and having no room to move is a mistake.
Buy Now vs. Make Offer
Buy Now: Best for lower-priced domains (under $2,000) where negotiation adds friction
Make Offer: Best for premium domains where price flexibility signals willingness to deal
Both simultaneously: List a Buy Now price but also enable offers — you get the fast sale option while still capturing negotiation upside

sections.heading: Common Domain Pricing Mistakes to Avoid
body: Overpricing Based on Sentiment

Your domain isn't worth more because you've held it for 10 years or because it took you time to register it. Buyers don't care about your investment timeline — they care about what the domain is worth to them.
Ignoring Renewal Costs
If your domain costs $15/year to renew and sits unsold for 5 years, that's $75 in holding costs. Factor renewal expenses into your pricing floor, especially on large portfolios.
Pricing Below Industry Minimums
Professional domain buyers rarely take anything under $500 seriously. Even a mediocre .com should be priced at $500 minimum. Below that, you're essentially giving it away.
Copying Asking Prices, Not Sales Prices

NameBio shows completed sales. Many sellers make the mistake of searching Afternic or Sedo for current listings and copying those prices — but those are asks, not closes. Always base your pricing on what domains actually sold for.

sections.heading: Real Pricing Examples
body: One-word .com — Characteristics: Dictionary word, broad appeal · Realistic Price Range: $10,000–$100,000+
Two-word .com — Characteristics: Keyword + noun, industry specific · Realistic Price Range: $1,500–$15,000
Brandable .com — Characteristics: Made-up, short, memorable · Realistic Price Range: $500–$5,000
Exact match keyword .com — Characteristics: High search volume keyword · Realistic Price Range: $2,000–$50,000
.net or .org equivalent — Characteristics: Same keywords, secondary TLD · Realistic Price Range: 25–50% of .com value

sections.heading: Final Checklist Before You List
body: [ ] Researched 5–10 comparable sales on NameBio
[ ] Run through at least one automated appraisal tool
[ ] Identified likely end-user categories and estimated their ROI
[ ] Factored in TLD weight
[ ] Set a minimum, target, and asking price
[ ] Chosen between Buy Now, Make Offer, or both

sections.heading: Expert Verdict
body: Domain pricing is a discipline that separates profitable sellers from those who either hold indefinitely or leave thousands of dollars on the table. The most common failure mode is emotional pricing — attaching a number to a domain based on how much the seller likes it, how long they've held it, or an automated tool's output taken at face value. None of these inputs reflect what a motivated buyer will actually pay.

The most reliable pricing methodology in 2026 combines NameBio comparable analysis (for market anchoring), end-user identification (for ceiling estimation), and the three-price framework (minimum, target, ask) to create a structured negotiation position. Sellers who internalize this process consistently close deals in a reasonable timeframe at prices that reflect genuine market value.

One critical insight that many beginners miss: the buyer who pays the most for your domain is almost never another domain investor. It's a business owner who needs the domain to power their brand or capture organic search traffic. Price for that buyer, communicate with that buyer in mind when writing your listing description, and the right offer will eventually arrive.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
body:
Q: How do I find out what my domain is worth?
A: Start with NameBio.com to research completed sales of similar domains. Search for domains with the same keywords, TLD, and approximate length. Run the domain through at least one automated appraisal tool (GoDaddy Appraisal or Estibot) as a cross-check. Finally, estimate the end-user value by identifying what type of business would buy it and what revenue that business could generate from owning it.

Q: What is a fair price for a two-word .com domain?
A: Two-word .com domains typically sell in the $1,500–$15,000 range depending on keyword strength, commercial intent, and industry demand. A generic combination like "FastDelivery.com" commands more than an obscure combination like "BluePebble.com." Research NameBio comparables for domains with similar keyword patterns to get a realistic range.

Q: Should I set a Buy Now price or Make Offer for my domain?
A: For domains priced under $2,000, a Buy Now price converts faster because it removes negotiation friction. For premium domains above $2,000, enabling Make Offer invites serious buyers to engage. The optimal setup for mid-range domains is to list both: a Buy Now price at the higher end of your range, with Make Offer enabled to capture buyers who negotiate.

Q: Why do domain appraisal tools give such different values?
A: Automated domain appraisal tools use algorithms that weight factors like keyword search volume, TLD, domain length, and historical sales data — but they struggle with brandability, market timing, and end-user demand. A short, invented word that a VC-funded startup desperately wants may be worth $50,000, but an algorithm will value it at $500. Use these tools as a baseline, not a ceiling.

Q: How does domain length affect pricing?
A: Shorter domains command higher prices, all else being equal. A five-letter .com is worth more than a ten-letter .com with equivalent keywords. This is because shorter domains are easier to type, remember, and brand. Four- and five-character .com domains (especially those with pronounceable vowel patterns) are valued by startup buyers and international investors for their scarcity.

Q: Can I raise my domain's price after listing it?
A: Yes. You can update your asking price at any time on Afternic, Sedo, or any other marketplace. If you've received multiple inquiries at your current price, raising the price slightly may be warranted. However, if a buyer has already been engaged in negotiation, raising the price mid-negotiation is considered poor form and will typically end the conversation. ---

articles.title: Domain Investing for Beginners: How to Start with $100
articles.description: Domain investing for beginners: learn how to start a domain portfolio with just $100, find undervalued names, and flip domains for profit. Practical guide inside.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Domain investing for beginners starts with a $100 budget to register 8–10 carefully chosen .com domains. Focus on short, memorable names with commercial appeal in growing industries. List them free on Afternic and Sedo. One successful flip in the $500–$2,000 range recoups your entire initial investment and proves the model works.

sections.heading: What Is Domain Investing?
body: Domain investing (also called domaining) is the practice of buying domain names at low cost and selling them later at a profit to businesses, startups, or other investors. Think of it like digital real estate. Just as physical land in the right location becomes more valuable over time, the right domain name gains value as industries grow and demand increases.
The best domain investors buy names before the market catches on — before a trend goes mainstream, before a startup in a space takes off, before a keyword becomes high-traffic.
How Much Can You Make?
Domain investing returns vary wildly:
Small flips: $50–$500 profit per domain
Mid-tier flips: $1,000–$10,000 per domain
Premium domain sales: $25,000–$100,000+
Beginners typically start with small flips and scale up as they develop market intuition.

sections.heading: What $100 Can Get You
body: At $100, you can register approximately 8–10 fresh domain names (at $8–$12 each). The key is choosing those 10 names carefully. One good sale can return your entire investment several times over.
Here's how to allocate a $100 starting budget:
Domain registrations (8–10 names) — Amount: $80–$100
NameBio access (optional for research) — Amount: Free tier available
Marketplace listing fees — Amount: $0 (Afternic, Sedo are free to list)
Your biggest investment at this stage isn't money — it's time spent on research.

sections.heading: Step 1: Learn What Makes a Domain Valuable
body: Before you spend a single dollar, understand what buyers actually want. This is the most important step for any domain investing beginner.
Characteristics of Valuable Domains
Short: Shorter is almost always better. A 5-character .com is more valuable than a 15-character one.
Memorable: The domain should be easy to say aloud and spell. If you have to repeat it twice on a phone call, it loses value.
No hyphens or numbers: "best-deals-4-you.com" is essentially worthless. Clean, pure letter domains are what buyers pay for.
Broad commercial appeal: "HomeInsuranceQuotes.com" has obvious buyers. "MattsPaintball2006.com" does not.
Strong TLD: .com dominates. Unless you have a compelling reason to go with another extension, stick to .com for your first portfolio.
Dictionary words: Real English words in domains carry inherent value. Made-up words must be short and catchy to have value.

sections.heading: Step 2: Find Undervalued Domains to Register
body: The gold rush of one-word .com domains is over — those were snapped up decades ago. But opportunities still exist for smart beginners.
Strategy 1: Emerging Industry Keywords

Watch for growing industries where keyword domains are still available. In the past, investors who registered domains like "CloudStorage.com" or "RemoteWork.com" before those terms went mainstream made fortunes.
Today, look at:
AI and machine learning subcategories
Green energy and sustainability niches
Longevity and health tech terms
Emerging financial products (DeFi, embedded finance)
Strategy 2: Two-Word Combinations
Two-word .com domains with clear commercial intent are still registerables. Look for patterns like:
[City] + [Service]: "AustinLandscaping.com"
[Adjective] + [Noun]: "SwiftInsurance.com"
[Industry] + [Tool]: "FreelanceInvoice.com"
Strategy 3: Expired Domain Hunting
Expired domains are names that previous owners didn't renew. Sometimes these have existing backlinks, traffic history, or brand recognition — making them more valuable than a fresh registration.
Use tools like:
ExpiredDomains.net: Free, massive database of expiring and expired names
NameJet: Auction platform for expired domains with backlinks
GoDaddy Auctions: Catch expired names being auctioned off

sections.heading: Step 3: Build Your First Domain Portfolio
body: A portfolio is simply the collection of domains you own. As a beginner, aim for quality over quantity.
The Right Portfolio Size for Beginners

Start with 5–10 carefully chosen domains rather than 50 mediocre ones. Every domain costs money to renew annually — a bad portfolio bleeds cash quietly. With 10 good names, you can focus on marketing them effectively.
Organizing Your Domain Portfolio
Keep a simple spreadsheet tracking:
Domain name
Registration date
Renewal cost and date
Estimated value
Where it's listed for sale
Any offers received
This discipline separates serious investors from hobbyists.

sections.heading: Step 4: List Your Domains for Sale
body: Once you've registered your domains, it's time to put them in front of buyers.
Where to List Domains
Afternic: Free to list, reaches buyers across 100+ partner registrars including GoDaddy. Best for passive reach.
Sedo: Free to list, strong international audience, includes a domain parking option to earn revenue while you wait.
Flippa: Broader marketplace that includes websites and apps — good for domains with existing traffic.
Dan.com: Clean, modern marketplace popular with end users and startups.
Pricing for Beginners
Start with a Buy Now price in the $500–$2,000 range for hand-registered domains. This is where most beginner sales happen. Premium names can be priced higher, but don't overprice fresh registrations.

sections.heading: Step 5: Flip Your First Domain
body: A domain flip is simply a sale. Your first flip is a major milestone — it proves the model works and teaches you more than any article ever can.
How to Speed Up Your First Sale

Outbound outreach: Research companies that might benefit from your domain and reach out directly via email or LinkedIn. This proactive approach often closes sales faster than waiting for inbound inquiries.
Domain forums: Post your domains on NamePros.com, the largest domain investing forum. Experienced investors and end-user buyers both hang out there.
Social media: LinkedIn is surprisingly effective for reaching business buyers. Share your domain listings in relevant industry groups.

sections.heading: What to Do with Your Profits
body: When your first domain sells, reinvest strategically:
1. Renew your best remaining domains: Keep the winners, drop the losers at renewal time
2. Scale your budget: Use profits to register more names or buy from the aftermarket
3. Invest in education: NamePros, DomainSherpa interviews, and domain investing podcasts are free

sections.heading: Common Mistakes Beginners Make
body: Buying What You Like Instead of What Sells
Personal taste doesn't matter in domaining. Your favorite niche might have no buyer pool. Always research demand before you register.
Registering Too Many Low-Quality Names
Ten domains at $10 each that nobody wants is $100 wasted plus $100/year in renewals. One great domain at $10 that sells for $2,000 is a 20,000% return.
Giving Up After 3 Months
Domain investing is a slow game. Most domains sell within 1–3 years. Beginners who quit after a few months never see the payoff from the research they already did.
Not Tracking Renewal Dates
Missing a renewal means losing a domain you paid to register. Use calendar reminders or enable auto-renew on your keeper names.

sections.heading: Expert Verdict
body: Domain investing remains one of the most accessible alternative investment categories available in 2026. The barrier to entry is genuinely low — a $100 investment, a free NameBio account for research, and free listings on Afternic and Sedo constitute a fully functional operation. No other investment class with comparable upside potential requires so little capital to start.

The critical success factor that separates profitable beginner investors from those who simply accumulate renewal costs is research discipline. Every domain registration decision should be preceded by NameBio comparables research to verify real buyer demand exists in that keyword space. Beginners who skip this step consistently build portfolios of names they personally find appealing rather than names with documented buyer demand.

For most beginners, the realistic expectation in year one is one or two sales in the $500–$2,000 range — enough to recover the initial investment and motivate continued development. The investors who stay in the game for two to five years and continuously improve their selection criteria are the ones who eventually achieve the four- and five-figure sales that make domaining genuinely life-changing.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
body:
Q: Is domain investing still profitable in 2026?
A: Yes. Domain investing remains profitable in 2026, though the days of easily registering valuable one-word .coms for $10 are over. Profitability now requires more research into emerging keyword categories (AI, clean energy, health tech), two-word commercial combinations, and expired domain opportunities. The aftermarket generates over $1 billion annually, and patient investors with good selection criteria continue to earn strong returns.

Q: How long does it take to sell a domain name?
A: Most hand-registered domains sell within 1–3 years when properly listed and priced. Some sell within weeks; others sit for years. Premium domains with strong commercial keywords and obvious end-user buyers tend to sell faster. Setting up outbound outreach to businesses in the relevant industry is the most effective way to accelerate the timeline.

Q: Do I need to build a website on my domains while I wait to sell them?
A: No. Most domain investors simply list their domains for sale on marketplaces without building anything on them. Adding a simple landing page ("This domain is for sale — contact us") can increase inbound inquiries, but it's not required. Sedo's domain parking option lets your domain display ads and generate passive revenue while it sits listed for sale.

Q: What are the best free tools for domain research?
A: The essential free tools for beginner domain research are: NameBio.com (completed sales database), ExpiredDomains.net (expiring domain search), Google Trends (keyword trend research), and the Wayback Machine at web.archive.org (checking what a domain was used for previously). These four tools are sufficient to research domains thoroughly before any investment.

Q: Is domain investing risky?
A: Domain investing carries real risk. Domains that don't sell still cost renewal fees every year. A 10-domain portfolio at $10/year per renewal costs $100/year even if nothing sells. The risk is manageable because the capital at stake is small — but it's real. The main risk mitigation strategy is quality selection: fewer, better-researched domains with documented buyer demand, rather than large portfolios of speculative names.

Q: Can I invest in domains part-time?
A: Absolutely. Most successful domain investors treat it as a part-time activity. The workflow — researching keywords, registering names, listing on marketplaces, and responding to inquiries — can be accomplished in a few hours per week. The passive nature of marketplace listings means your domains are working for you even when you're not actively engaged.

Q: What is the minimum budget to start domain investing?
A: You can technically start with $10 for a single domain registration. However, a $100 starting budget is recommended because it allows enough registrations (8–10) to develop pattern recognition through varied research and selection. With one domain, a bad selection wastes your entire budget. With 10 domains, you learn from each decision and increase the odds of having at least one strong performer. ---

articles.title: Best Domains to Invest In for 2026 (Trending TLDs and Keywords)
articles.description: Discover the best domains to invest in for 2026. Explore trending TLDs, profitable keywords, and domain investment strategies driving returns this year.

sections.heading: Overview
body: The best domains to invest in for 2026 are short .com and .ai domains in AI, clean energy, mental health, and fintech keyword categories. Four- to six-character brandable .coms, exact-match industry keywords, and geo-service combinations in mid-sized cities offer the strongest combination of acquisition cost and end-user demand in the current market.

sections.heading: Why 2026 Is a Strong Year for Domain Investing
body: Several macro forces are converging to create strong demand for specific domain categories:
AI expansion: Every week, new AI-powered products launch and need a name
Small business digitization: Millions of local businesses still lack a professional online presence
Startup funding rebound: As venture capital flows back into tech, new companies need premium domains
Regulatory changes in financial services and healthcare: New compliance categories create new keyword demand
Creator economy growth: Individual creators, newsletters, and communities all need branded homes
Understanding these forces tells you where to look for the best domains to invest in 2026.

sections.heading: Trending TLDs to Watch in 2026
body: .com: Still King, Always King

Nothing has dethroned .com, and nothing will in 2026. Premium .com domains continue to set records at auction. If you're buying a domain as a pure investment, .com is always the safest and highest-returning TLD.
That said, specific subcategories within .com are especially hot:
Short (4–6 character) .coms
Brandable one-word .coms
Industry-specific two-word .coms (especially in AI, health, and finance)
.ai: The Hottest Extension in Tech

The .ai TLD (technically Anguilla's country code) has become the standard for artificial intelligence products. In 2026, demand for .ai domains continues to accelerate. Companies building AI tools are willing to pay premium prices for clean, memorable .ai domains.
Examples of valuable .ai patterns:
[Function].ai (Generate.ai, Analyze.ai)
[Industry].ai (Legal.ai, Medical.ai)
[Short brandable].ai (Kira.ai, Nova.ai)
If you can find short, clean .ai domains still available, they represent strong investment candidates.
.io: Still Relevant for Tech Startups

The .io extension remains popular in developer tools, SaaS products, and fintech. While .ai has taken some of its shine, .io maintains a loyal audience in technical startup communities. Two-word .io domains in the developer and API tooling space are particularly sought after.
.co: The Global Business Extension

.co has stabilized as a credible alternative for international businesses that can't get their preferred .com. Startups in Latin America, Europe, and Asia often prefer .co. Short, clean .co domains with global commercial appeal hold their value.
.health and .clinic: Regulated Niche Extensions

Healthcare is one of the fastest-growing sectors online. New TLDs like .health, .clinic, and .care are gaining traction with medical practices, telehealth companies, and wellness brands that want to signal their niche instantly in the domain itself.

sections.heading: Hottest Keyword Categories for 2026
body: Beyond TLDs, keyword themes drive the most profitable domain investment trends. Here are the categories generating the most end-user demand.
Artificial Intelligence Keywords
Any domain incorporating AI-related terms has strong potential:
GPT, AI, LLM, neural, vision, voice, agent, autonomous
[Verb]AI.com patterns: WriteAI.com, SortAI.com, BuildAI.com
[Industry]AI.com: LegalAI.com, HealthAI.com, FinanceAI.com

The challenge is that obvious AI domains are already taken or priced expensively. Look for less obvious combinations in emerging AI subcategories: AI safety, AI governance, AI content detection, synthetic data.
Sustainability and Clean Energy
ESG investing, carbon credits, and renewable energy are multi-decade trends. Domains in this space that still show up as available include combinations around:
Solar, wind, carbon, offset, neutral, green, sustainable, circular
[City]Solar.com, [State]WindEnergy.com
CarbonOffset[Noun].com patterns
Businesses in this space are growing rapidly and often lack professional online branding.
Mental Health and Wellness
Mental health awareness has exploded since 2020 and shows no signs of slowing. Telehealth platforms, therapy apps, and wellness coaches all need domains. Look for:
Anxiety, therapy, mindfulness, burnout, resilience, wellbeing
[Condition]Help.com, [Type]Therapy.com
OnlineCounseling[Niche].com patterns
Financial Technology
Fintech continues to generate enormous demand for clean domains:
Embedded finance, BNPL (buy now pay later), digital banking, crypto compliance
[Service]Pay.com, [Country]FinTech.com
Neobank, digital wallet, open banking keyword combinations
Remote Work and the Future of Work
Remote-first companies and distributed teams need tools, communities, and brands. Domains around:
RemoteTeams, AsyncWork, DistributedHR
Virtual office, remote hiring, freelance management
These have solid end-user buyer pools in HR tech and SaaS

sections.heading: Domain Length and Pattern Trends
body: Short Domains Are Getting Shorter (and More Expensive)

Four- and five-letter .com domains have essentially all been registered. But six- and seven-letter brandables are still findable with effort. These clean, pronounceable, vowel-balanced names are what startups pay $5,000–$50,000+ for.
LLLL.com and LLLLL.com

Four and five-letter .com combinations (all letters, no numbers) are consistently in demand from Chinese investors and global startup buyers. If you can acquire these at reasonable prices, they hold value well.
Geo + Service Combinations

Despite predictions of their decline, local geo-domain combinations remain strong. A city-specific service domain like "ChicagoRoofing.com" or "MiamiSEO.com" has a clear, motivated buyer — the local business owner who wants to dominate local search.

sections.heading: Profitable Domain Investment Strategies for 2026
body: The Trend Scout Strategy

Follow tech newsletters, startup launch pages, and VC portfolio announcements. When you see a new category emerging — say, "AI agents" in early 2025 — register keyword domains in that space before they go mainstream.
The Expiry Sniper Strategy

Use tools like ExpiredDomains.net and NameJet to identify domains with real traffic history or backlinks that are expiring. A domain that already ranks or receives visitors is worth more than a fresh registration.
The Geo-Service Arbitrage Strategy

Register local service domains in mid-sized cities before local businesses wise up to their value. A dental practice or law firm will pay $1,000–$5,000 for a clean geo-service domain if it means owning their local keyword.
The Brandable Flip Strategy

Register short, made-up, pronounceable names and list them on marketplaces like BrandBucket or Sedo. Startups buy these constantly for their company name. Prices range from $1,500 to $10,000+ for clean brandables.

sections.heading: Red Flags: What NOT to Invest In
body: Even in a hot market, some domains will never sell:
Hyphenated domains: "Best-Domain-Names.com" is nearly worthless
Trademarked terms: Registering variations of brand names creates legal liability
Long, complex strings: More than 15 characters dramatically reduces value
Obscure TLDs: Extensions like .guru or .rocks have limited buyer pools
Typo domains: Search engines and browsers have largely eliminated typo traffic

sections.heading: Expert Verdict
body: The domain investment landscape in 2026 is more stratified than at any previous point. The top tier — short .coms, clean .ai domains, and premium brandables — commands prices that reflect genuine scarcity and proven end-user demand. Below that tier, the market is selective but accessible: investors who understand keyword trends and research buyer demand before registering can still identify names that will sell at 50x–200x their registration cost.

The dominant trend shaping the best 2026 domain investments is the continued AI industry expansion. Unlike previous technology waves, AI is not limited to one vertical — it is creating new buyer demand for domains in healthcare, legal, finance, education, marketing, and dozens of other sectors simultaneously. An investor who registers keyword-appropriate .com or .ai domains across multiple AI-adjacent niches is positioned to benefit from whichever sector's AI adoption moves fastest.

The clearest strategic recommendation for 2026 is to avoid betting exclusively on a single trend or TLD. Build a diversified portfolio across .com brandables, .ai tech domains, and geo-service combinations. This approach balances short-term flip potential with longer-term asset appreciation, and gives you exposure to multiple buyer categories — startups, local businesses, and enterprise technology companies — rather than depending on a single buyer pool.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
body:
Q: Are .ai domains a good investment in 2026?
A: Yes, .ai domains are among the strongest investment opportunities in 2026. The explosive growth of AI-powered products has created intense demand for clean, memorable .ai domains. Short [brandable].ai and [industry].ai patterns are particularly sought after by startups. The risk is that the obvious .ai keywords are already registered — successful investment requires finding less obvious combinations in emerging AI subcategories.

Q: What makes a domain name valuable as an investment?
A: A domain's investment value comes from commercial keyword relevance, length (shorter is more valuable), TLD quality (.com commands the highest premium), memorability and pronunciability, and the size of the end-user buyer pool for that keyword. Domains at the intersection of high buyer demand and genuine scarcity — short, clean, relevant .coms — consistently appreciate over time.

Q: Is .com still the best TLD to invest in?
A: .com remains the strongest TLD for investment purposes in 2026. It commands the highest sale prices, has the broadest buyer base, and is the only TLD that end users across all industries and geographies actively seek. .ai is a strong secondary investment TLD specifically for technology sector domains, but .com should constitute the majority of any investment portfolio.

Q: How do I find domain investment opportunities in 2026?
A: Monitor tech newsletters, startup launch pages, and VC portfolio announcements for emerging keyword categories. Use ExpiredDomains.net to find expiring names with traffic history. Search NameBio for keyword categories with a history of sales to verify buyer demand. Follow domain investing communities on NamePros and DomainSherpa for intelligence on what categories are generating sales.

Q: What is the best domain investment strategy for a small budget?
A: With a small budget, focus on two-word .com registrations in a single trending keyword category (AI, clean energy, or mental health). Register 5–8 names with clear commercial intent and obvious end-user buyers. List them on Afternic and Sedo immediately. Supplement with outbound outreach to businesses in the relevant industry. This targeted approach generates better returns than spreading a small budget across many unrelated speculative names.

Q: Are geo-service domains still worth investing in?
A: Yes. Geo-service .com domains remain a consistently undervalued category. Local businesses in growing cities are motivated, identified buyers who understand the direct revenue value of owning their city + service keyword. A domain like "DenverSolarInstall.com" has an obvious buyer pool of solar installation companies in Denver — which is a more predictable buyer than hoping a startup finds your brandable domain on a marketplace.

Q: What domains should I avoid buying as investments?
A: Avoid hyphenated domains, domains with numbers, trademarked terms, obscure TLDs with limited buyer audiences (such as .guru, .rocks, or .biz), domains over 15 characters, and domains in declining industries with shrinking buyer pools. Also avoid typo domains — browser autocorrect and search engine navigation have effectively eliminated the traffic value that made typo domains valuable a decade ago. ---

articles.title: How Domain Escrow Works (And Why You Should Always Use It)
articles.description: Learn how domain escrow works, why it protects both buyers and sellers, and when to use Escrow.com for safe domain transfers. Complete guide inside.

sections.heading: Overview
body: Domain escrow works by having a neutral third party (typically Escrow.com) hold the buyer's payment until the seller transfers the domain and the buyer confirms receipt. Neither party controls both the money and the domain simultaneously, eliminating the risk of fraud on either side. It costs 3.25% or less of the transaction value.

sections.heading: What Is Domain Escrow?
body: Escrow is a financial arrangement where a neutral third party holds funds during a transaction until both parties fulfill their obligations. In domain name transactions, escrow works like this:
1. The buyer sends payment to the escrow service (not to the seller)
2. The seller transfers the domain to the buyer
3. The buyer confirms receipt of the domain
4. The escrow service releases the funds to the seller

At no point does either party control both the money and the domain simultaneously. This structure eliminates the biggest risk in private domain transactions: someone taking the money (or the domain) and disappearing.

sections.heading: Why Domain Transactions Are High-Risk Without Escrow
body: Domain transfers happen digitally, between people who often don't know each other, for amounts that can range from $500 to $500,000. This combination creates an environment ripe for fraud.
Common Domain Transaction Scams
The "Transfer First" Request: A fake buyer pressures you to transfer the domain first, promising to pay immediately after. Once you transfer, they vanish.
Fake Payment Proof: A scammer sends you a forged PayPal screenshot or bank transfer confirmation. The domain leaves your account; the money never arrives.

Chargeback Fraud: A buyer pays via credit card or PayPal, receives the domain, then files a chargeback claiming they never received it. PayPal sides with the buyer and you lose both the domain and the money.
Overpayment Scams: A buyer sends a check for more than the asking price and asks for a refund of the difference. The check bounces later. You've sent real money back; they sent nothing.
Domain escrow eliminates all of these risks because funds are verified before the transfer happens, and they're held by a regulated third party.

sections.heading: How Escrow.com Domain Transactions Work (Step by Step)
body: Escrow.com is the most widely used and trusted escrow service for domain name transactions. Here's exactly how the process flows.
Step 1: Both Parties Agree to Use Escrow
The buyer and seller agree to the domain name, price, and currency. Either party can initiate the escrow transaction on Escrow.com.
Step 2: Create the Transaction
One party (usually the seller) logs into Escrow.com and creates a new transaction. You'll enter:
Domain name
Agreed sale price
Inspection period (typically 5 days)
Who pays the escrow fee (buyer, seller, or split)
Step 3: Buyer Funds the Escrow Account

Escrow.com notifies the buyer, who then deposits the agreed amount into the escrow account. Accepted payment methods include wire transfer, credit card, PayPal, and check. Escrow.com verifies the funds before any domain movement begins.
Step 4: Seller Transfers the Domain

Once Escrow.com confirms the funds are secured, the seller initiates the domain transfer to the buyer. This typically involves pushing the domain (if both parties use the same registrar) or initiating a standard domain transfer with an EPP/authorization code.
Step 5: Buyer Inspects and Accepts
The buyer has the agreed inspection period (usually 5 business days) to verify the domain has transferred correctly and functions as expected. They log into Escrow.com and click "Accept."
If something is wrong — the domain didn't transfer, or it's not what was described — the buyer can dispute the transaction during the inspection period, and Escrow.com mediates.
Step 6: Funds Released to Seller
Once the buyer accepts, Escrow.com releases the funds to the seller (minus the escrow fee). The transaction is complete.

sections.heading: How Much Does Escrow.com Cost?
body: Escrow.com charges a fee based on the transaction size. The fee can be paid by the buyer, the seller, or split between both — this is negotiated as part of the deal.
Approximate Escrow.com Fee Schedule
$0–$5,000 — Approximate Fee: 3.25% (minimum $30)
$5,001–$25,000 — Approximate Fee: $162.50 + 0.26% of amount over $5,000
Over $1,000,000 — Approximate Fee: Negotiated
For context, on a $2,000 domain sale, the escrow fee is approximately $65. On a $10,000 sale, it's approximately $175. This cost is absolutely worth the protection it provides.

sections.heading: Alternatives to Escrow.com
body: While Escrow.com is the gold standard, there are a few other options for safe domain transfers.
Marketplace-Integrated Escrow

Many domain marketplaces (Afternic, Sedo, Dan.com) have their own built-in escrow systems. When a sale completes through one of these platforms, the escrow process is handled automatically. You don't need a separate Escrow.com account.
This is one of the reasons listing on a marketplace is generally safer than selling privately — the protection is built in.
Flippa Escrow
The Flippa marketplace, which handles domain and website sales, uses Escrow.com as its integrated payment solution. Transactions initiated through Flippa flow through Escrow.com automatically.
PayPal (Not Recommended)

PayPal is sometimes used for small domain transactions, but it carries serious risk for sellers. PayPal's buyer protection policies make it easy for fraudulent buyers to file chargebacks even after receiving a domain. Avoid PayPal for domain transactions whenever possible.

sections.heading: When Is Escrow Especially Critical?
body: Escrow is always a good idea, but it's absolutely non-negotiable in these situations:
High-value domains: Any domain above $1,000 should use escrow. The cost is minimal compared to the protection.
Private sales: Transactions outside established marketplaces have no built-in protection mechanism.
Unfamiliar buyers or sellers: If you don't personally know and trust the other party, escrow protects everyone.
International transactions: Cross-border payments have additional fraud risk and slower recourse options.
Domains with existing traffic or revenue: The domain's value is higher and verification is more complex — escrow's inspection period gives you time to confirm everything transferred correctly.

sections.heading: Red Flags That Should Trigger Escrow Insistence
body: If any of the following happen during a domain negotiation, insist on escrow or walk away:
The buyer or seller resists using escrow ("it's not necessary, I'm legit")
They suggest an escrow service you've never heard of and can't verify
They want to pay via wire transfer directly to your personal account
They ask you to transfer the domain before payment clears
They're in an unusual rush and pressuring you to skip steps
Legitimate buyers and sellers have no reason to avoid escrow. Anyone who does is either a scammer or has done enough transactions to know they're asking you to take a risk.

sections.heading: Safe Domain Transfers: A Quick Checklist
body: [ ] Both parties agree on escrow before any transfer begins
[ ] Transaction is created on Escrow.com or through a reputable marketplace
[ ] Buyer funds escrow with a verified payment method
[ ] Seller receives confirmation from Escrow.com before initiating transfer
[ ] Domain transfer is initiated through registrar's official transfer process
[ ] Buyer verifies domain receipt during inspection period
[ ] Funds released only after buyer acceptance

sections.heading: Expert Verdict
body: Domain escrow is not optional for any transaction above trivial amounts — it is the minimum acceptable standard of due diligence for buyers and sellers in the domain market. The fraud patterns described in this guide are documented, recurring, and entirely preventable. Every year, sellers lose thousands of dollars to chargeback fraud and fake payment proof, and buyers lose domains to sellers who vanish after receiving payment. Every single one of these losses could have been prevented with a $65–$175 escrow arrangement.

The argument against escrow is always some version of speed or trust: "we're in a hurry" or "I'm a known seller." Neither holds up to scrutiny. Escrow.com processes most domain transactions in under a week, and the inspection period is configurable. As for trust — legitimate parties in a legitimate transaction have absolutely nothing to lose by using escrow and everything to gain. Resistance to escrow is the single most reliable fraud signal in domain transactions.

For sellers operating through established marketplaces (Afternic, Sedo, Dan.com), the platform's built-in escrow provides equivalent protection automatically. For anyone conducting a private sale — found through a forum post, cold outreach, or personal referral — Escrow.com is non-negotiable. The fee is a cost of doing business; it is not negotiable away for the sake of saving $65.

sections.heading: Frequently Asked Questions
body:
Q: Is Escrow.com safe to use for domain transactions?
A: Escrow.com is the most trusted escrow service for domain transactions, licensed as a money transmitter, and recommended by ICANN. It has processed over $5 billion in transactions. The service verifies buyer funds before any domain transfer begins, protects sellers against chargebacks, and mediates disputes during the inspection period. It is the industry standard for safe domain transactions.

Q: Who pays the escrow fee — buyer or seller?
A: The escrow fee is negotiated between buyer and seller as part of the deal. Common arrangements include the buyer pays, the seller pays, or both split it 50/50. Neither arrangement is standard — it's whatever both parties agree to. Many marketplace transactions (through Sedo or Afternic) absorb the escrow cost within the platform commission.

Q: Can I use PayPal for a domain sale instead of escrow?
A: PayPal is strongly discouraged for domain transactions above $100. PayPal's buyer protection policies allow buyers to file chargebacks claiming "item not received" or "not as described" — and domains, as digital goods, are difficult to defend in PayPal disputes. Sellers routinely lose the domain and the money in fraudulent PayPal domain transactions. Use Escrow.com instead.

Q: What happens if the buyer doesn't accept the domain during the inspection period?
A: If the buyer does not accept the domain and does not dispute the transaction during the inspection period, Escrow.com automatically releases the funds to the seller after the period expires. If the buyer disputes, Escrow.com reviews the evidence from both parties and mediates the dispute. Sellers are protected from arbitrary refusal to accept a legitimate transfer.

Q: Do domain marketplaces like Sedo and Afternic have their own escrow?
A: Yes. Sedo, Afternic, Dan.com, and most major domain marketplaces include built-in escrow processes that automatically protect both parties. When a sale completes through a marketplace, the platform handles payment verification, domain transfer monitoring, and fund release without requiring a separate Escrow.com account. This is one of the primary advantages of selling through a marketplace rather than privately.

Q: How long does an escrow domain transaction take?
A: A typical Escrow.com domain transaction takes 5–10 business days from initiation to fund release. This includes the buyer funding escrow (1–3 days depending on payment method), the domain transfer (1–3 days), and the buyer's inspection period (5 business days, though buyers often accept faster). Wire transfer funding is the fastest payment method for initiating the transaction. ---
